lessons.title: Gas Behaviour Experiments
lessons.description: Investigate the three gas laws using controlled experiments, graphs and fully worked A2 calculations.
learning_objectives: Describe controlled experiments relating p, V and T for a fixed mass of gas.
Use absolute pressure and kelvin temperature correctly.
Interpret gas-law graphs and apply the combined gas law.
Evaluate practical limitations and percentage uncertainty.

slides.title: Start here: what can change in a gas?
slides.content:
A bicycle pump becomes harder to compress as its trapped air occupies less space. A sealed tyre can have a higher pressure on a warm day. These observations involve three measurable quantities: pressure p, volume V and thermodynamic temperature T. The aim of this lesson is to investigate their relationships without changing several things at once.

You will describe three experiments for a fixed mass of gas, choose useful graphs, and apply the resulting gas laws. Read the apparatus explanations before the calculations: a formula is reliable only when its experimental conditions are satisfied. This lesson assumes you can rearrange equations and find a straight-line gradient.

QuantitySI unitMeaning
Pressure ppascal, PaForce per unit area exerted on a wall
Volume Vcubic metre, m³Space occupied by the gas
Temperature Tkelvin, KTemperature measured from absolute zero

“Fixed mass” means the same gas stays inside the apparatus: no leaks, added gas or escape. Pressure in a gas equation is absolute pressure, measured relative to a vacuum. A gauge may instead report pressure above the atmosphere; check its mode before using its reading.

Tutor check-in

A syringe leaks during compression. Which essential condition is lost?

slides.title: Temperature and pressure: prepare the numbers
slides.content:
Gas-law temperature ratios must use kelvin. A change from 20 °C to 40 °C is a rise of 20 K, but it is not a doubling of thermodynamic temperature. Convert an individual temperature using T in kelvin = θ in degrees Celsius + 273.15. For the numerical gas-law examples in this lesson, use the stated school approximation T = θ + 273.

pabsolute = pgauge + patmospheric

Worked example 1: a pressure gauge reads 45.0 kPa above atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere is at 101 kPa and the gas is at 27 °C. Prepare SI data for a gas equation.

Step 1: Identify the reference of the gauge. Its reading is the extra pressure above the atmosphere, so add the atmospheric pressure.

Step 2: Calculate pabsolute = 45.0 + 101 = 146 kPa.

Step 3: Convert kilopascals to pascals: p = 146 × 10³ = 1.46 × 10⁵ Pa.

Step 4: Convert the temperature with the stated approximation: T = 27 + 273 = 300 K.

Check: The absolute pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure, and the kelvin temperature is positive. The gauge value alone would underestimate the pressure.

For a ratio calculation, both volumes may be expressed in the same unit because their conversion factors cancel. When evaluating a constant with SI units, or using R or k in later lessons, convert volume to m³: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³ and 1 litre = 10⁻³ m³.

Tutor check-in

A gas warms from 20 °C to 40 °C. Which temperature ratio belongs in a gas law?

slides.title: Boyle’s law: the apparatus and a fair method
slides.content:
Seal a gas syringe and connect it to an absolute-pressure sensor with a short airtight tube. Clamp the apparatus securely and check that a steady volume gives a steady pressure. The independent variable is the trapped volume; the dependent variable is pressure. Keep the mass of gas and its temperature constant.

Move the piston a small distance with the screw, then wait for the pressure to settle before recording the volume and pressure. Repeat over several well-separated volumes without exceeding the apparatus pressure limit. Take repeat readings, including readings while increasing volume again, to reveal leaks, piston friction or failure to reach thermal equilibrium.

Rapid compression does work on the gas and can warm it. A reading taken immediately afterwards tests more than the pressure–volume relationship. Make each change slowly and allow energy transfer to the surroundings before recording. The room acts as a temperature reservoir; merely working in the same room does not guarantee that the gas is already at room temperature.

Use the total trapped volume. The connecting tube and sensor cavity contain gas too. Add their calibrated volume to the syringe reading, or design the apparatus so that this correction is negligible compared with every measured volume. An omitted fixed volume produces a systematic distortion, especially at small syringe volumes.

slides.title: Boyle’s law: the graph and the calculation
slides.content:
At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of an approximately ideal gas is inversely proportional to its volume. Doubling the volume halves the pressure. Therefore the product pV is constant; pressure against volume gives a decreasing curve, while pressure against reciprocal volume gives a straight line through the origin within uncertainty.

pV = constant   ⇒   p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
p = (pV)constant × 1V

Worked example 2: the same gas occupies 60.0 cm³ at 100 kPa. It is compressed slowly to 40.0 cm³ and allowed to return to its original temperature. Find the new absolute pressure.

Step 1: Choose Boyle’s law because mass and temperature are fixed.

Step 2: Rearrange p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ by dividing both sides by V₂: p₂ = p₁V₁V₂.

Step 3: Use the same volume unit for the ratio: p₂ = 100 × 60.040.0 = 150 kPa.

Step 4: State the answer as absolute pressure: 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa.

Check: The volume has fallen to two-thirds of its original value, so pressure rises by a factor of 1.5. A lower pressure would contradict the controlled experiment.

Tutor check-in

The piston is pushed in rapidly and the pressure is read at once. Why may the result sit above a Boyle’s-law prediction?

slides.title: Pressure–temperature experiment: hold volume fixed
slides.content:
Seal a fixed mass of gas inside a rigid bulb connected to an absolute-pressure sensor. Immerse the bulb in a stirred water bath and measure the bath temperature with a separate thermometer. The independent variable is temperature and the dependent variable is absolute pressure; gas mass and container volume are controlled.

Begin at a suitable low bath temperature. Stir gently, wait until the thermometer and pressure readings are steady, and record both. Warm the bath in small stages and repeat. Use several temperatures across a safe range; do not heat a sealed apparatus beyond its rating. Take repeats and check the room-temperature reading again afterwards for evidence of a leak or drift.

The thermometer measures the bath, not automatically the gas. Waiting and good immersion reduce a temperature difference. Gas in tubing outside the bath may remain at a different temperature, so minimise this connecting volume. The bulb must be sufficiently rigid that its thermal expansion is small compared with the measurement uncertainty.

pT = constant   ⇒   p₁T₁ = p₂T₂

Plot absolute pressure against kelvin temperature. An ideal relationship is a straight line through the origin; its gradient is the constant pressure divided by temperature. A Celsius plot is still straight but its extrapolated zero-pressure intercept is near −273 °C. The experiment does not cool a real gas all the way to that intercept.

slides.title: Pressure–temperature law: work through the ratio
slides.content:
Worked example 3: gas in a rigid sealed container has an absolute pressure of 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa at 17 °C. Find its pressure at 77 °C, assuming ideal behaviour.

Step 1: Convert both temperatures: T₁ = 17 + 273 = 290 K and T₂ = 77 + 273 = 350 K.

Step 2: The mass and volume are fixed, so use equal pressure-to-kelvin-temperature ratios.

Step 3: Multiply by T₂ to isolate the new pressure: p₂ = p₁ × T₂T₁.

Step 4: Substitute p₂ = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 350290 = 1.2069… × 10⁵ Pa.

Step 5: Round to three significant figures: p₂ = 1.21 × 10⁵ Pa.

Check: The thermodynamic temperature rises by about 21%, so the pressure rises by about 21%. The much larger Celsius ratio would give an implausible answer.

The same law lets you infer a temperature from pressure, but it cannot identify a leak. If pressure falls at unchanged volume and temperature, loss of gas is a possible explanation. Check experimental conditions before selecting the equation.

Tutor check-in

For a pressure–temperature experiment, which container is appropriate?

slides.title: Volume–temperature experiment: hold pressure fixed
slides.content:
Trap a short column of dry air in a horizontal, uniform-bore capillary with one sealed end and a small mobile oil plug. Keep the open end above the water-bath surface. Air on the open side of the plug communicates with the atmosphere. The independent variable is temperature and the dependent variable is trapped-air volume; gas mass and pressure should stay fixed.

Place the trapped-air section in a stirred bath. At each temperature, allow the gas to equilibrate and measure the length of the air column from the sealed end to the inner face of the oil plug. Keep the tube horizontal so that the plug has no substantial vertical hydrostatic pressure difference across it. Use a short, freely moving plug and check that it does not stick or leak air.

With cross-sectional area A constant, V = Aℓ. Thus length is proportional to volume and may be used as the measured variable. Account for a significant rounded-end volume by calibration; the simple V = Aℓ model assumes it is negligible. A changing bore would invalidate a direct length–volume comparison.

VT = constant   ⇒   V₁T₁ = V₂T₂

Plot V against T in kelvin, or ℓ against T if the bore is uniform. Expect a straight line through the origin within uncertainty and the ideal-gas approximation. Atmospheric pressure should stay approximately steady during the experiment; a stuck plug can prevent the trapped gas from remaining at atmospheric pressure.

slides.title: Volume–temperature law: use a length measurement
slides.content:
Worked example 4: a uniform-bore capillary traps an air column of length 8.00 cm at 27 °C. Find its length at 87 °C when pressure is unchanged. Neglect the sealed-end volume.

Step 1: Convert the temperatures: T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 360 K using the stated approximation.

Step 2: Because V = Aℓ and A is unchanged, equal volume-to-temperature ratios become equal length-to-temperature ratios.

Step 3: Isolate ℓ₂: ℓ₂ = ℓ₁ × T₂T₁.

Step 4: Substitute ℓ₂ = 8.00 × 360300 = 9.60 cm.

Check: The temperature increases by 20% on the kelvin scale, so both length and volume increase by 20%. Cross-sectional area cancels; there is no need to invent its value.

Tutor check-in

Why must the capillary have a uniform bore?

slides.title: Read the graphs and combine the laws
slides.content:
A curve on a p–V graph can suggest an inverse relationship, but a straight p–reciprocal-V graph gives a clearer test. Use a best-fit line across the data and a large gradient triangle. Check intercepts and scatter; do not force a line through the origin simply because the theory predicts it. A nonzero intercept may reveal an offset or an omitted volume.

Worked example 5: two well-separated points on a best-fit p against reciprocal-V line are (2.00 × 10⁴ m⁻³, 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa) and (5.00 × 10⁴ m⁻³, 2.50 × 10⁵ Pa). Find the gradient and interpret it.

Step 1: Find the changes: Δp = 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa and Δ(1 divided by V) = 3.00 × 10⁴ m⁻³.

Step 2: Calculate gradient = 1.50 × 10⁵3.00 × 10⁴ = 5.00 Pa m³.

Step 3: Compare p = (pV)constant × reciprocal V with y = mx. The gradient equals the constant pV.

Step 4: Since 1 Pa m³ = 1 J, the gradient may also be expressed as 5.00 J.

Check: Its unit is pressure times volume. Using the gradient of the curved p–V graph would not give this constant.

For a fixed mass, the three laws combine into a single statement. It allows both pressure and volume to change, provided the amount of gas stays fixed.

pVT = constant   ⇒   p₁V₁T₁ = p₂V₂T₂

slides.title: Combined changes and practical judgement
slides.content:
Worked example 6: a fixed mass of gas changes from 120 kPa, 2.00 litres and 300 K to 350 K and 1.50 litres. Find the new pressure.

Step 1: Both volume and temperature change, so use the combined gas law.

Step 2: Multiply by T₂ and divide by V₂: p₂ = p₁ × V₁V₂ × T₂T₁.

Step 3: Substitute consistent units: p₂ = 120 × 2.001.50 × 350300 = 186.666… kPa.

Step 4: Round to three significant figures: p₂ = 187 kPa.

Check: Compression and heating both raise the pressure. Each factor is greater than one, so the result should exceed 120 kPa.

Distinguish scatter from bias. Repeating a reading and averaging can reduce random uncertainty, but it does not remove a pressure-sensor zero error, an uncorrected tube volume or a consistently different bath and gas temperature. Explain how a proposed improvement addresses the actual source of error.

At a syringe volume of 20.0 ± 0.5 cm³, the percentage volume uncertainty is 2.5%. At 60.0 ± 0.5 cm³ it is about 0.83%. Small volumes magnify both relative reading uncertainty and the importance of dead volume. A broad range improves a graph, but include only conditions for which the apparatus model remains credible.

Tutor check-in

Repeating a Boyle’s-law measurement ten times gives closely agreeing readings. What can you conclude?

slides.title: A2 practice: laws and data
slides.content:
These are original A2-style questions. The suggested marks are teaching guidance, not an official CCEA mark scheme. Attempt each question before revealing its worked solution.

Question 1: Slow compression [4 marks]

Gas at 95.0 kPa occupies 72.0 cm³. Find its pressure at 48.0 cm³ if mass and temperature remain fixed.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Use p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ because temperature and gas mass stay fixed.

Step 2: p₂ = 95.0 × 72.048.0 = 142.5 kPa.

Step 3: To three significant figures, p₂ = 143 kPa. The smaller volume produces a higher pressure.

Question 2: Rigid-container heating [4 marks]

A sealed rigid container is at 100 kPa and 22 °C. What Celsius temperature corresponds to 125 kPa? Use T = θ + 273.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: T₁ = 22 + 273 = 295 K. Use the pressure–temperature law at fixed volume.

Step 2: T₂ = T₁ × p₂p₁ = 295 × 125100 = 368.75 K.

Step 3: θ₂ = 368.75 − 273 = 95.75 °C, approximately 95.8 °C.

Question 3: Two changes at once [5 marks]

A fixed mass initially occupies 3.00 litres at 100 kPa and 300 K. It reaches 400 K and 150 kPa. Calculate its final volume.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Use equal pV-to-T ratios; isolate V₂ = V₁ × p₁p₂ × T₂T₁.

Step 2: V₂ = 3.00 × 100150 × 400300 = 2.666… litres.

Step 3: V₂ = 2.67 litres. Heating tends to expand the gas, but the pressure increase is the larger factor.

slides.title: A2 practice: experiment design and review
slides.content:
Question 4: Omitted tube volume [4 marks]

A syringe reads 20.0 cm³ initially and 40.0 cm³ finally. Its connecting tube contains 5.0 cm³ of gas. The initial absolute pressure is 200 kPa. Predict the final pressure at constant temperature and explain why using the syringe readings alone is wrong.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: The total initial volume is 25.0 cm³; the total final volume is 45.0 cm³.

Step 2: p₂ = 200 × 25.045.0 = 111.1… kPa, approximately 111 kPa.

Step 3: Syringe readings alone would give 100 kPa. They omit gas that is also compressed and therefore exaggerate the volume ratio.

Question 5: Describe a controlled experiment [6 marks]

Describe a method to investigate pressure against temperature for a fixed mass at constant volume. Include two controls or precautions and the graph you would use.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Use a sealed rigid bulb connected to an absolute-pressure sensor, immersed in a stirred water bath with a thermometer.

Step 2: Change bath temperature in stages. At each stage stir and wait for steady temperature and pressure; record paired readings and repeat across a range.

Step 3: Check airtightness to keep gas mass fixed; use a rigid bulb and minimise connecting gas outside the bath. These address leaks, volume changes and temperature mismatch.

Step 4: Convert temperatures to kelvin and plot absolute pressure against T. A straight line through the origin within uncertainty supports p proportional to T.

Question 6: Relative uncertainty [4 marks]

A volume reading is 25.0 ± 0.5 cm³ and pressure is 120 ± 2 kPa. Estimate the maximum percentage uncertainty in their product pV.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: For a product, add the input percentage uncertainties in a maximum-uncertainty estimate.

Step 2: Volume uncertainty = 0.525.0 × 100% = 2.0%. Pressure uncertainty = 2120 × 100% = 1.67%.

Step 3: Total ≈ 3.7%. This estimates reading uncertainty and does not automatically include omitted tube volume or sensor calibration bias.

Before moving on: say which quantities must stay fixed for each law, explain why temperatures and pressures need the correct reference, and describe how each apparatus achieves its control. In the next lesson, pV = nRT introduces the amount of gas explicitly.

lessons.title: Ideal Gas Equation
lessons.description: Use pV = nRT with SI units, molar mass and changing gas amounts, with fully worked A2 applications.
learning_objectives: Use pV = nRT to calculate pressure, volume, amount and temperature.
Convert units and sample mass to amount using molar mass.
Choose between the full ideal-gas equation and the fixed-mass combined law.
Explain the main limitations of the ideal-gas model.

slides.title: From a fixed-mass law to pV = nRT
slides.content:
The previous lesson found that pV divided by T is constant for a fixed mass of gas. Different samples need not have the same constant: twice as much gas at the same temperature and volume produces twice the pressure. The ideal gas equation includes the amount of substance n explicitly.

pV = nRT

Here p is absolute pressure in Pa, V is volume in m³, n is amount of substance in mol, T is thermodynamic temperature in K and R is the molar gas constant. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for this lesson’s calculations, and use T = θ + 273 when a Celsius temperature is supplied. Use the constants stated by an examination question if they differ in precision.

One mole contains the same specified number of particles, whatever the substance. Mole is an amount unit, not a mass unit: a mole of helium and a mole of nitrogen have different masses. The next lesson connects n to the actual number of particles.

Tutor check-in

Two ideal-gas samples have the same volume and temperature. One contains twice the number of moles. Its pressure is:

slides.title: The ideal model and SI preparation
slides.content:
An ideal gas is a model in which particle volume is negligible compared with container volume and intermolecular forces do not contribute appreciably between collisions. Real gases approximate it best at relatively low pressure and sufficiently high temperature, away from condensation. At high pressure, finite molecular size matters; at low temperature, attractions become more significant. “Ideal” describes an approximation, not a special substance.

Given quantityPreparationCommon error
Pressure in kPaMultiply by 10³ and use absolute pressureUsing the gauge reading without adding atmospheric pressure
Volume in litresMultiply by 10⁻³ to obtain m³Using litres with an SI value of R
Volume in cm³Multiply by 10⁻⁶ to obtain m³Converting a volume as though it were a length
Temperature in °CAdd 273 here to obtain KUsing Celsius in a gas equation
Mass in gramsConvert to kg if molar mass is in kg mol⁻¹Mixing gram and kilogram units

The units provide a useful check: Pa m³ equals joules, while mol × J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × K also equals joules. R must match the pressure, volume and temperature units you use. Keeping SI units throughout avoids a hidden conversion factor.

Tutor check-in

Which is the correct conversion of 250 cm³?

slides.title: Worked example: find the amount of gas
slides.content:
Worked example 1: gas occupies 2.50 litres at an absolute pressure of 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 27 °C. Calculate the amount of gas.

Step 1: List SI data: V = 2.50 × 10⁻³ m³, p = 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa and T = 300 K.

Step 2: Choose pV = nRT because pressure, volume and temperature are known and n is required.

Step 3: Divide both sides by RT: n = pVRT.

Step 4: Substitute n = (1.20 × 10⁵)(2.50 × 10⁻³)8.31 × 300 = 3002493 = 0.120337… mol.

Step 5: Round to three significant figures: n = 0.120 mol.

Check: The numerator is 300 J and the denominator is 2493 J mol⁻¹, leaving mol. Enter the whole denominator in calculator brackets.

Keep extra digits while working and round at the end. A calculator entry that divides by R and then multiplies by T is not the same as dividing by the product RT. Write the rearranged equation before entering numbers.

Tutor check-in

When rearranging pV = nRT for n, which denominator is correct?

slides.title: Worked example: find pressure or temperature
slides.content:
Worked example 2: a rigid 4.00 × 10⁻³ m³ container holds 0.200 mol of ideal gas at 350 K. Calculate its absolute pressure.

Step 1: Identify the unknown p and keep V in m³.

Step 2: Divide the ideal gas equation by V: p = nRTV.

Step 3: Substitute p = 0.200 × 8.31 × 3504.00 × 10⁻³ = 145425 Pa.

Step 4: Round to p = 1.45 × 10⁵ Pa.

Check: At unchanged n and T, making the container smaller would increase pressure. The unit J divided by m³ is Pa.

Worked example 3: 0.100 mol occupies 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa. Find the gas temperature in kelvin and degrees Celsius.

Step 1: Divide pV = nRT by nR: T = pVnR.

Step 2: Calculate T = (1.50 × 10⁵)(2.00 × 10⁻³)0.100 × 8.31 = 361.010… K.

Step 3: State T = 361 K. Convert the unrounded value using θ = T − 273, giving approximately 88.0 °C.

Check: The kelvin value must be obtained before the Celsius conversion. Substituting 88 into the gas equation would fail to reproduce the stated pressure.

slides.title: Mass, molar mass and gas density
slides.content:
A question may give the gas mass instead of its amount. Let msample denote total sample mass and M denote molar mass. Their units must match. Dividing the mass by the mass of one mole gives the number of moles.

n = msampleM

Worked example 4: 5.60 g of nitrogen, of molar mass 28.0 g mol⁻¹, is at 300 K and 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate its volume.

Step 1: Calculate n = 5.6028.0 = 0.200 mol. The gram units cancel because both masses use grams.

Step 2: Rearrange pV = nRT: V = nRTp.

Step 3: Substitute V = 0.200 × 8.31 × 3001.00 × 10⁵ = 4.986 × 10⁻³ m³.

Step 4: State V = 4.99 × 10⁻³ m³ = 4.99 litres.

Check: Using 5.60 as n would confuse grams with moles and greatly overestimate the volume.

As an application, insert n = msample divided by M into the gas equation and divide by V. Since density ρ = msample divided by V, this gives p = ρRT divided by M. With M in kg mol⁻¹, density follows in kg m⁻³.

ρ = pMRT

For nitrogen at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K, M = 0.0280 kg mol⁻¹ gives ρ = 1.12 kg m⁻³. This derived relationship is useful when mass and volume are involved; it follows from the same ideal model.

Tutor check-in

A gas has molar mass 32.0 g mol⁻¹. Which value belongs in an SI density calculation?

slides.title: Choosing the equation when conditions change
slides.content:
For two states of the same sealed sample, n and R are unchanged. Dividing pV = nRT by T gives the combined gas law. This is often quicker than first finding n, but its shortcut depends on the gas amount staying fixed.

p₁V₁T₁ = p₂V₂T₂   for n₁ = n₂

If gas enters or leaves, use the full equation in each state. For example, in a rigid tank held at constant temperature, pressure is proportional to n. A rise in pressure can then result from adding gas rather than warming it. A question that says “a valve is opened” should prompt you to check the mass condition.

Worked example 5: a 0.0100 m³ tank is maintained at 300 K. Its absolute pressure rises from 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa to 1.50 × 10⁵ Pa as gas is added. Find the amount added.

Step 1: Write p₁V = n₁RT and p₂V = n₂RT; V and T are unchanged.

Step 2: Subtract the equations: (p₂ − p₁)V = (n₂ − n₁)RT.

Step 3: Calculate Δn = (5.00 × 10⁴)(0.0100)8.31 × 300 = 0.200561… mol.

Step 4: State Δn = 0.201 mol added.

Check: The positive pressure change gives a positive amount added. Treating n as fixed would wrongly predict a temperature change.

Tutor check-in

A sealed rigid ideal-gas tank doubles its absolute pressure without losing gas. What has happened to T?

slides.title: A2 practice: direct and mass-based calculations
slides.content:
These original questions use suggested teaching marks. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T = θ + 273. Try the calculation before revealing the steps.

Question 1: Amount in a container [4 marks]

A 1.50 litre container holds gas at 200 kPa and 300 K. Calculate n.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Convert p = 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa and V = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m³.

Step 2: n = pVRT = 3008.31 × 300 = 0.120337… mol.

Step 3: n = 0.120 mol to three significant figures.

Question 2: Mass to pressure [5 marks]

A 2.00 g helium sample, of molar mass 4.00 g mol⁻¹, occupies 0.0100 m³ at 27 °C. Calculate its absolute pressure.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: n = 2.004.00 = 0.500 mol and T = 300 K.

Step 2: p = nRTV = 0.500 × 8.31 × 3000.0100 = 124650 Pa.

Step 3: p = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa. Mass is first converted into amount; it cannot replace n directly.

Question 3: Temperature from mass [5 marks]

A 4.48 g sample of nitrogen of molar mass 28.0 g mol⁻¹ occupies 4.00 litres at 100 kPa. Find T and θ.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: n = 4.4828.0 = 0.160 mol; V = 4.00 × 10⁻³ m³ and p = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa.

Step 2: T = pVnR = 4000.160 × 8.31 = 300.842… K.

Step 3: T ≈ 301 K and θ ≈ 27.8 °C using the unrounded temperature and the stated conversion.

slides.title: A2 practice: evaluate the model and choose a method
slides.content:
Question 4: Changing the amount [5 marks]

A rigid tank at constant temperature has an absolute pressure of 180 kPa. After gas escapes, its pressure is 120 kPa. Calculate the fraction of the initial amount remaining and explain why the fixed-mass combined law cannot be used.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: At fixed V and T, p = nRT divided by V, so n is proportional to absolute pressure.

Step 2: Fraction remaining = n₂n₁ = 120180 = 23. One-third has escaped.

Step 3: The combined fixed-mass law assumes n₁ = n₂. That condition has been broken.

Question 5: Evaluate an answer [4 marks]

A student substitutes V = 500, p = 100 and T = 20 into n = pV divided by RT, using R = 8.31, for a sample of volume 500 cm³ at 100 kPa and 20 °C. Identify and correct the three input errors.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Convert volume: 500 cm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

Step 2: Convert pressure: 100 kPa = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa, assumed absolute.

Step 3: Convert temperature: 20 °C = 293 K here. Correct n = 50.08.31 × 293 = 0.0205 mol.

Question 6: Ideal-gas limitations [3 marks]

Explain why a real gas near condensation at high pressure is less accurately described by pV = nRT.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: At high pressure particles are close together, so their own volume is less negligible compared with the gas volume.

Step 2: Near condensation, attractive intermolecular forces substantially affect the motion and pressure.

Step 3: The ideal model neglects these effects. A numerical ideal-gas answer in these conditions should be treated as an approximation.

Ready to continue? You should be able to prepare SI data, isolate an unknown before substitution, convert mass to moles and decide whether n stays fixed. Next, pV = NkT describes the same gas in terms of individual particles.

lessons.title: Alternative Gas Equation
lessons.description: Connect moles to particle counts and use pV = NkT, with A2 examples of number density and mass density.
learning_objectives: Relate N and n using Avogadro’s constant.
Show the equivalence of pV = nRT and pV = NkT.
Calculate particle count, pressure, volume, temperature and number density.
Distinguish particle count, number density and mass density.

slides.title: Count particles instead of moles
slides.content:
The ideal gas equation pV = nRT describes a sample using its amount in moles. We can also describe the same sample using the number of individual particles N. An atom counts as one particle in helium; an N₂ molecule counts as one particle in nitrogen. Do not count its two atoms as two independently moving gas molecules.

Avogadro’s constant NA links these descriptions. In this lesson use NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The Boltzmann constant k plays the particle-level role that R plays at mole level. Rounded values are appropriate here; use a question’s supplied precision when answering it.

N = nNA    and    n = NNA
R = NAk   ⇒   pV = NNA × NAkT = NkT

The alternative equation is therefore pV = NkT. It expresses the same ideal-gas model, with the same requirements for absolute pressure, SI volume and kelvin temperature. N is a pure particle count, so it has no mol unit.

Tutor check-in

In pV = NkT for nitrogen gas, N counts:

slides.title: Understand k and prepare a calculation
slides.content:
The product kT has units of joules. Multiplying it by the particle count gives an energy unit, matching pV. This does not yet mean that kT is the complete kinetic energy of one molecule; the numerical connection to mean translational kinetic energy is developed later.

SymbolMeaningValue or unit
NNumber of particlesDimensionless count
nAmount of substancemol
NAParticles per mole6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ here
kBoltzmann constant1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ here
RMolar gas constantApproximately 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

As a consistency check, the rounded product NAk is 8.3076 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, which rounds to 8.31. Small final-digit differences between answers obtained with rounded constants do not indicate different physical laws.

Worked example 1: a helium sample contains 0.150 mol. Find its number of particles and identify what those particles are.

Step 1: Use N = nNA because the amount in moles is given.

Step 2: Calculate N = 0.150 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²².

Step 3: State the result as 9.03 × 10²² helium atoms, with no mol unit attached to N.

Check: A fraction of a mole contains fewer than Avogadro’s number of particles. Helium gas is monatomic, so atoms are the appropriate particles.

Tutor check-in

What is the unit of kT?

slides.title: Worked example: infer the particle count
slides.content:
Worked example 2: an ideal gas at 300 K occupies 500 cm³ at an absolute pressure of 100 kPa. How many particles does it contain?

Step 1: Convert V = 500 × 10⁻⁶ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and p = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa.

Step 2: Rearrange pV = NkT by dividing by kT: N = pVkT.

Step 3: Evaluate the numerator: pV = (1.00 × 10⁵)(5.00 × 10⁻⁴) = 50.0 J.

Step 4: Evaluate the denominator: kT = (1.38 × 10⁻²³)(300) = 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Step 5: Calculate N = 50.04.14 × 10⁻²¹ = 1.2077… × 10²², or 1.21 × 10²² particles.

Check: J divided by J leaves a count. The very small energy scale per particle means that a macroscopic sample contains an enormous number of particles.

You can check this against the mole equation: n = 0.0201 mol and nNA is approximately 1.21 × 10²². Write the full scientific-notation denominator in calculator brackets. Dividing by 1.38 and then multiplying by 10⁻²³ reverses the intended power-of-ten operation.

Tutor check-in

Which pair of quantities belongs together in an ideal-gas equation?

slides.title: Worked examples: pressure and number density
slides.content:
Worked example 3: 2.00 × 10²² particles occupy 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 350 K. Calculate their absolute pressure.

Step 1: Use p = NkTV because the particle count is supplied.

Step 2: The numerator is (2.00 × 10²²)(1.38 × 10⁻²³)(350) = 96.6 J.

Step 3: p = 96.61.00 × 10⁻³ = 9.66 × 10⁴ Pa.

Check: The product of the powers of ten is 10⁻¹ before multiplying by the remaining numbers. Energy divided by volume gives pressure.

Number density means particles per unit volume, not mass per unit volume. Divide pV = NkT by VkT to find it. Its unit is m⁻³ because a particle count is dimensionless.

NV = pkT

Worked example 4: find the number density at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K.

Step 1: Choose the rearranged expression N divided by V = p divided by kT.

Step 2: Substitute NV = 1.00 × 10⁵(1.38 × 10⁻²³)(300) = 2.4154… × 10²⁵ m⁻³.

Step 3: State the number density as 2.42 × 10²⁵ particles per cubic metre.

Check: The earlier 500 cm³ sample has this number density multiplied by 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³, reproducing about 1.21 × 10²² particles. The container volume is not needed to find the density.

slides.title: What equal pressure and temperature do tell you
slides.content:
For ideal gases at equal pressure and temperature, N divided by V is equal. Equal volumes under those same conditions therefore contain equal numbers of gas particles, regardless of molecular species. Their mass densities need not be equal because their particles can have different masses.

The equation concerns a collective sample. It does not say that all particles have the same speed or that a particle count can be read from one collision. Later, kinetic theory will explain pressure as the combined effect of many collisions and link temperature to a mean kinetic energy.

Tutor check-in

Equal volumes of ideal helium and nitrogen have the same p and T. What must be equal?

slides.title: A2 practice: microscopic gas calculations
slides.content:
These are original A2-style questions with suggested teaching marks. Use k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Question 1: Particle count from amount [3 marks]

How many molecules are in 0.0250 mol of nitrogen?

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: N = nNA = 0.0250 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²².

Step 2: To three significant figures this is 1.51 × 10²² N₂ molecules. It is not twice this number; N counts molecules here.

Question 2: Volume from particle count [4 marks]

A sample contains 1.00 × 10²³ particles at 300 K and an absolute pressure of 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa. Find its volume.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Isolate V = NkTp.

Step 2: NkT = (1.00 × 10²³)(1.38 × 10⁻²³)(300) = 414 J.

Step 3: V = 4142.00 × 10⁵ = 2.07 × 10⁻³ m³, or 2.07 litres.

Question 3: Temperature from microscopic data [4 marks]

A sealed sample has 5.00 × 10²² particles in 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. Find T.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Use T = pVNk. The numerator pV is 240 J.

Step 2: Nk = (5.00 × 10²²)(1.38 × 10⁻²³) = 0.690 J K⁻¹.

Step 3: T = 2400.690 = 347.826… K, or 348 K.

slides.title: A2 practice: counts, mass and review
slides.content:
Question 4: Number density and mass density [5 marks]

At 100 kPa and 300 K, an ideal gas has particle mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Find its number density and mass density.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Number density = pkT = 1.00 × 10⁵(1.38 × 10⁻²³)(300) = 2.42 × 10²⁵ m⁻³.

Step 2: Mass density is number density times mass per particle: ρ = NVm.

Step 3: Using the unrounded count density gives ρ = 1.123… kg m⁻³, or 1.12 kg m⁻³.

Question 5: Explain the equivalence [4 marks]

Show how pV = nRT becomes pV = NkT, and explain the meanings of n and N.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: n is amount in mol; N is particle count. They obey N = nNA.

Step 2: Substitute n = NNA and R = NAk.

Step 3: pV = NNA × NAkT = NkT. The particles-per-mole factor cancels.

Before continuing: distinguish n, N and N divided by V; pair R with moles and k with particles. Next, internal energy connects microscopic motion and interactions to energy changes in a sample.

lessons.title: Internal Energy
lessons.description: Explain microscopic kinetic and potential energy, energy distributions and changes by heating or work.
learning_objectives: Define internal energy in terms of microscopic kinetic and interaction potential energy.
Distinguish temperature, internal energy and macroscopic energy stores.
Explain the distribution of particle energies and changes of state.
Track simple energy transfers using an explicitly stated sign convention.

slides.title: What is stored inside a material?
slides.content:
A warm metal block stores energy even when it is stationary on a bench. Its atoms are moving microscopically and interacting with neighbours. Internal energy U is the sum of the random microscopic kinetic energies and the interaction potential energies of the particles in a system. It is an extensive quantity: more material can contain more internal energy at the same temperature.

Microscopic kinetic energy includes the permitted random modes of particle motion. Depending on the material, these may include translation, rotation and vibration. Potential energy arises from interactions and relative positions; it is not a second name for temperature. We usually calculate a change in internal energy rather than assign an absolute value to all microscopic potential energies.

The kinetic energy of the whole block sliding along the bench, and its gravitational potential energy when lifted as a whole, are macroscopic energy stores. They are not the random microscopic energy counted in U. You must state the system and distinguish its bulk motion from motion relative to its centre of mass.

Tutor check-in

A room-temperature metal block is lifted onto a shelf without changing its temperature or state. Which store definitely increases?

slides.title: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
slides.content:
In a solid, particles vibrate about relatively fixed equilibrium positions. Their motion has kinetic energy, while changes in their separations alter interaction potential energy. A solid’s particles are therefore not stationary merely because the solid keeps its shape.

In a liquid, particles remain close but can move past one another. Both motion and interactions contribute to internal energy. In a gas, particles travel through much larger separations; their translational kinetic energy is especially important. Real gas interactions can still contribute potential energy.

For an ideal gas, intermolecular interaction energy is neglected between collisions. This simplifies the model, but it does not imply that every molecule has the same energy. Nor does it remove possible rotational and vibrational modes inside molecules. The later formula involving three-halves kT refers specifically to mean translational kinetic energy.

Tutor check-in

Why can a solid have internal kinetic energy while it is stationary?

slides.title: Temperature is not total internal energy
slides.content:
Temperature tells us about the thermal state. In the classical ideal-gas model it is proportional to mean translational kinetic energy per particle. Internal energy adds contributions from all particles, so temperature alone cannot specify its total. Amount of material, substance, state and available modes of motion matter too.

At one temperature, an equilibrium gas has a distribution of particle speeds and energies: some move faster than others, and collisions continually redistribute energy. The temperature relation concerns the average across many particles. Random motion means there is no preferred direction for a gas at rest; it does not mean all speeds are equal.

Worked example 1: two samples of the same monatomic ideal gas are at the same temperature. Sample B contains twice as many particles as sample A. Compare their mean translational kinetic energies and total internal energies.

Step 1: Equal temperature gives equal mean translational kinetic energy per particle in this model.

Step 2: For a monatomic ideal gas, internal energy is the sum of those translational kinetic energies; intermolecular interaction energy is neglected.

Step 3: Twice the particle count, with the same mean energy per particle, gives UB = 2UA.

Check: A larger total store does not require a larger temperature. This conclusion uses the stated same-substance, monatomic ideal-gas model.

A cup and a bath of water can be at the same temperature while the bath has a much larger thermal energy capacity. For different substances or states, avoid inferring a total-energy comparison from temperatures alone.

Tutor check-in

At equilibrium, all gas molecules must have identical kinetic energy. Is this correct?

slides.title: Heating, work and energy bookkeeping
slides.content:
Energy can cross the system boundary by heating or by work. Heating is energy transfer associated with a temperature difference; it is not a substance stored inside the block. Electrical work on a heater inside the system or mechanical compression can also increase internal energy. Cooling and expansion work can decrease it.

A useful supporting energy balance is ΔU = Q + Won, where Q is net energy transferred into the system by heating and Won is net work done on it. The signs must be stated: outward heating is negative Q; work done by the system is negative Won. This bookkeeping explains energy changes; the core topic here is the microscopic meaning of U.

Worked example 2: a gas receives 600 J by heating and does 250 J of mechanical work on its surroundings. Calculate its internal-energy change.

Step 1: Choose the gas as the system.

Step 2: The inward heating is Q = +600 J. Work done by the gas means Won = −250 J.

Step 3: Calculate ΔU = 600 − 250 = +350 J.

Step 4: Interpret the positive result: the gas has gained 350 J of internal energy.

Check: The full 600 J is not stored in the gas because 250 J crosses the boundary as outward work.

Worked example 3: during compression, 180 J of work is done on a gas while 70 J leaves by heating. Find ΔU.

Step 1: Work done on the gas gives Won = +180 J.

Step 2: Outward heating gives Q = −70 J.

Step 3: ΔU = −70 + 180 = +110 J.

Check: Compression can increase internal energy even without inward heating. Always identify the direction of each transfer.

slides.title: Energy changes can occur at constant temperature
slides.content:
During melting at the melting temperature, energy supplied can increase internal energy while temperature remains approximately constant. The energy changes the microscopic arrangement and interaction potential energy as particles become less constrained. It is therefore wrong to use “temperature unchanged” as proof that internal energy cannot change.

Away from a change of state, heating a fixed mass usually raises temperature and the mean microscopic kinetic energy. During a change of state, a substantial potential-energy change can occur instead. The energy needed for a phase change is distinct from the Q = mcΔθ calculation studied in the final lesson of this section.

Worked example 4: 2.40 kJ is delivered to a sample during melting at constant temperature. Assume negligible losses and negligible macroscopic work. Explain the internal-energy change.

Step 1: Convert the energy supplied: 2.40 kJ = 2400 J.

Step 2: With no significant loss or macroscopic work, the sample gains ΔU ≈ +2400 J.

Step 3: The temperature does not rise, so an increase in temperature-related mean kinetic energy is not the explanation.

Step 4: The increase is associated with the changed particle arrangement and interaction potential energy during melting.

Check: A constant-temperature plateau can still involve energy transfer and an increase in internal energy. No specific-heat formula should be used to predict the melting energy.

Tutor check-in

A pure substance melts at constant pressure and temperature while absorbing energy. What is the best explanation?

slides.title: A2 practice: explain the microscopic stores
slides.content:
These are original A2-style questions with suggested teaching marks. For energy balances, take inward heating and work done on the stated system as positive.

Question 1: Define and distinguish [4 marks]

Define internal energy and explain why the kinetic energy of a moving train is not itself the internal energy of the train.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Internal energy is the sum of random microscopic kinetic energies and interaction potential energies of the particles.

Step 2: Bulk train motion is coherent macroscopic motion of the system as a whole.

Step 3: It differs from the random motion and interactions within the train. The train has internal energy as well as bulk kinetic energy.

Question 2: Distribution of energies [3 marks]

Two ideal-gas samples have the same temperature. Explain what can be said about mean translational kinetic energy and individual particle energies.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Their mean translational kinetic energy per particle is equal.

Step 2: Individual energies span a distribution and need not equal the mean.

Step 3: Equal temperature does not imply that every particle in either sample has the same speed or energy.

Question 3: Heating during melting [4 marks]

A sample absorbs 850 J while melting at steady temperature. Explain why its internal energy can increase.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Internal energy contains both microscopic kinetic and interaction potential energy.

Step 2: Constant temperature does not require constant interaction potential energy.

Step 3: Energy changes particle arrangement during melting; with negligible losses and work, ΔU ≈ +850 J.

slides.title: A2 practice: follow the transfers
slides.content:
Question 4: Expansion balance [4 marks]

A gas receives 900 J by heating and does 320 J of work on its surroundings. Find ΔU and explain your sign choice.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Q = +900 J because heating transfers energy into the gas.

Step 2: Won = −320 J because the gas does work outward.

Step 3: ΔU = 900 − 320 = +580 J. The stored internal energy increases.

Question 5: Cooling under compression [4 marks]

A gas loses 150 J by heating while 90 J of work is done on it. Find ΔU. Does compression guarantee a temperature rise?

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Q = −150 J and Won = +90 J.

Step 2: ΔU = −150 + 90 = −60 J.

Step 3: Compression alone does not guarantee warming: in this balance more energy leaves by heating than enters by work. For a fixed monatomic ideal gas, the negative ΔU corresponds to a lower temperature.

Before moving on: distinguish temperature from total U, describe microscopic motion in each state, and explain an energy change without simply saying “heat is stored”. Next, kinetic theory connects wall collisions to macroscopic pressure.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory Equation
lessons.description: Connect wall collisions to gas pressure through microsteps, then use mean-square speed and rms speed in A2 calculations.
learning_objectives: State the assumptions of the ideal-gas kinetic model.
Explain momentum transfer, collision rate and the isotropy factor in the pressure equation.
Use pV = one-third Nm⟨c²⟩ and its density form.
Distinguish mean speed, mean squared speed and rms speed.

slides.title: Pressure comes from many wall collisions
slides.content:
A gas pushes on the walls of its container because its particles repeatedly collide with them. Each rebound changes a particle’s momentum. The equal and opposite momentum transfer to the wall produces a force; force per area is pressure. Kinetic theory links this collective effect to molecular mass and motion.

pV = 13Nm⟨c²⟩

Here N is the number of gas particles, m is the mass of one particle in kg, and ⟨c²⟩ is the mean of the squared particle speeds in m² s⁻². The angle brackets denote a mean over the particles. V is in m³ and p is absolute pressure in Pa. The product Nm is total gas mass.

CCEA A2 requires you to use this relationship. The following collision argument provides supporting reasoning so that its factors and assumptions make sense. It uses Newtonian mechanics, an ideal gas and averages over many collisions.

Tutor check-in

In this kinetic-theory equation, m means:

slides.title: State the assumptions before using the model
slides.content:
Treat the gas as a very large collection of small particles moving randomly. Their own volume is negligible compared with the container volume. Between collisions they experience negligible intermolecular forces, so travel at constant velocity. Collisions with the walls are elastic: the appropriate velocity component reverses with no loss of translational kinetic energy in the model.

At equilibrium in a gas with no bulk flow, motion is isotropic: no spatial direction is preferred. The mean squared velocity component is therefore the same along x, y and z. Individual particles still have different speeds and directions. Isotropy concerns the distribution, not identical trajectories.

We consider a cubic container of side L and wall area A = L². Its volume is V = AL. A particle’s velocity components are ux, uy and uz, and its speed satisfies c² = ux² + uy² + uz². The x component alone determines collisions with a wall perpendicular to x.

Tutor check-in

What does “elastic collision with a wall” mean in this model?

slides.title: Microstep 1: momentum transferred in one rebound
slides.content:
Take rightward as positive and consider a particle approaching the right wall with ux > 0. Its incident x momentum is +mux. After an elastic rebound it is −mux. Subtract initial from final to find the molecule’s momentum change.

Δpx,molecule = (−mux) − (+mux) = −2mux

By Newton’s third law, the wall receives the opposite impulse, +2mux. The factor two comes from reversal, not from there being two particles. A reversal from +ux to −ux changes velocity by twice its initial magnitude.

Worked example 1: a particle of mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg strikes a wall with normal velocity component +400 m s⁻¹ and rebounds elastically. Find its momentum change and the impulse delivered to the wall.

Step 1: Initial x momentum is +mux and final x momentum is −mux.

Step 2: Δpx,molecule = −2 × (4.65 × 10⁻²⁶) × 400 = −3.72 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹.

Step 3: The wall receives +3.72 × 10⁻²³ N s. These are equal magnitudes with opposite directions.

Check: Impulse and momentum change have equivalent units. Reversal produces a factor two rather than a factor one.

slides.title: Microsteps 2–3: collision rate and force
slides.content:
In the simplified single-particle argument, successive visits to the same wall involve a journey to the opposite wall and back. The distance along x is 2L, not L. The time between those visits is 2L divided by ux. We use this regular-wall-collision argument to obtain a mean force; the equilibrium many-particle result remains the relevant model when molecules also collide with one another.

Δt = 2Lux

Average force is momentum transferred per unit time. Divide the wall impulse by the interval. The two factors of two cancel, and the second ux enters because a faster normal motion increases the collision frequency as well as the impulse per collision.

Fone particle = 2muxΔt = 2mux × ux2L = mux²L

For N particles with possibly different x components, add their individual contributions. The sum of their ux² values is N times the mean squared x component.

F = Nm⟨ux²⟩L

This is the force on one wall, averaged over enough collisions for a steady pressure to make sense. It uses squared components: the signed mean velocity of an equilibrium gas is zero, but its mean square is positive.

Tutor check-in

Why is the return-trip distance 2L rather than L?

slides.title: Microsteps 4–5: divide by area and use isotropy
slides.content:
Pressure is F divided by A. Since the cube volume is AL, dividing the force expression by area replaces LA by V. This yields a relationship involving one mean squared component.

p = FA = Nm⟨ux²⟩LA = Nm⟨ux²⟩V

Now average the identity c² = ux² + uy² + uz². Isotropy makes the three mean squared components equal, so each is one-third of the mean squared speed. This is where the factor one-third enters.

⟨c²⟩ = 3⟨ux²⟩   ⇒   ⟨ux²⟩ = ⟨c²⟩3
p = Nm⟨c²⟩3V   ⇒   pV = 13Nm⟨c²⟩

The dimensional check is useful: kg × m² s⁻² gives J on the right, and Pa m³ gives J on the left. The equation does not require all particles to have one speed; it explicitly uses a mean square over the distribution.

Tutor check-in

The factor one-third comes from:

slides.title: Root-mean-square speed is a different average
slides.content:
The root-mean-square speed crms is the square root of ⟨c²⟩. To find it, square each speed, take the mean of those squares, then take a square root. It is generally different from the ordinary arithmetic mean speed ⟨c⟩. Squaring the mean speed does not reproduce the mean squared speed.

crms = √⟨c²⟩    and    ⟨c²⟩ = crms²

Worked example 2: three illustrative particles have speeds 2.00, 4.00 and 6.00 m s⁻¹. Find the mean speed and rms speed. These deliberately small numbers demonstrate the calculation; they are not room-temperature gas measurements.

Step 1: The mean speed is 2 + 4 + 63 = 4.00 m s⁻¹.

Step 2: Square the individual speeds: 4, 16 and 36 m² s⁻².

Step 3: Mean square = 4 + 16 + 363 = 18.666… m² s⁻².

Step 4: Take the square root: crms = √18.666… = 4.32 m s⁻¹.

Check: The rms speed is greater than the ordinary mean for this spread of speeds. The mean square has squared-speed units; its square root has speed units.

Use crms² where the kinetic-theory equation contains ⟨c²⟩. Do not insert crms alone, which would give the wrong units.

Tutor check-in

A gas has crms = 500 m s⁻¹. What is ⟨c²⟩?

slides.title: Use density to make the equation practical
slides.content:
Total gas mass is Nm, so density is ρ = Nm divided by V. Substitute this into the pressure expression to obtain a convenient form when density and rms speed are known.

p = 13ρcrms²   ⇒   crms = √(3pρ)

Worked example 3: a gas has density 1.20 kg m⁻³ and rms speed 500 m s⁻¹. Calculate its pressure.

Step 1: Choose p = one-third × ρ × crms².

Step 2: Square the speed first: 500² = 2.50 × 10⁵ m² s⁻².

Step 3: p = 13 × 1.20 × 2.50 × 10⁵ = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa.

Check: The result is of the order of atmospheric pressure. Forgetting the square would give both an incorrect number and incorrect dimensions.

Worked example 4: gas of density 1.60 kg m⁻³ is at 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate its rms speed.

Step 1: Rearrange p = one-third × ρ × crms² to crms² = 3pρ.

Step 2: Calculate crms² = 3 × 1.20 × 10⁵1.60 = 2.25 × 10⁵ m² s⁻².

Step 3: Take the square root to obtain crms = 474.34… ≈ 474 m s⁻¹.

Check: The value before the square root is a squared speed, not a speed. Keep the factor three in the numerator.

slides.title: A2 practice: compute from microscopic motion
slides.content:
These original A2-style questions have suggested teaching marks. Distinguish molecular mass m from total mass Nm, and show the square-root step when finding rms speed.

Question 1: Pressure from particles [4 marks]

A 0.0100 m³ container holds 2.00 × 10²³ particles of mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. Their rms speed is 500 m s⁻¹. Calculate p.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Nm = (2.00 × 10²³)(4.65 × 10⁻²⁶) = 9.30 × 10⁻³ kg.

Step 2: p = Nm crms²3V = (9.30 × 10⁻³)(500²)3 × 0.0100.

Step 3: p = 7.75 × 10⁴ Pa.

Question 2: Find rms speed [4 marks]

An ideal gas has density 1.25 kg m⁻³ and absolute pressure 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa. Find crms.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: crms² = 3pρ = 3.00 × 10⁵1.25 = 2.40 × 10⁵ m² s⁻².

Step 2: crms = √(2.40 × 10⁵) = 489.898… m s⁻¹.

Step 3: To three significant figures, crms = 490 m s⁻¹.

Question 3: A change in speed [3 marks]

At unchanged particle number, particle mass and volume, rms speed increases by 10%. By what percentage does pressure increase?

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Pressure is proportional to crms² under the stated fixed conditions.

Step 2: Speed factor = 1.10, so pressure factor = 1.10² = 1.21.

Step 3: Pressure increases by 21%, not 10%.

slides.title: A2 practice: explain the factors
slides.content:
Question 4: Normal momentum change [4 marks]

A molecule strikes a smooth wall with normal velocity +uₓ and leaves with −uₓ. Explain the factor two in its momentum change and the factor one-third in the full pressure equation.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Momentum change is final minus initial: (−muₓ) − (+muₓ) = −2muₓ.

Step 2: The wall receives the opposite impulse. The factor two comes from reversal of the normal velocity component.

Step 3: The factor one-third comes from isotropy: the three mean squared velocity components are equal and sum to ⟨c²⟩.

Question 5: Mean square versus squared mean [4 marks]

Two particles have speeds 300 and 500 m s⁻¹. Calculate ⟨c²⟩ and cᵣₘₛ and show why using the square of their ordinary mean is wrong.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: ⟨c²⟩ = 300² + 500²2 = 170000 m² s⁻².

Step 2: crms = √170000 = 412.31… ≈ 412 m s⁻¹.

Step 3: Ordinary mean speed = 400 m s⁻¹; its square is 160000 m² s⁻², which differs from 170000.

Before moving on: explain the factor two, the collision-rate step and the factor one-third; then calculate with either particle count or density. In the next lesson, comparing this equation with pV = NkT links temperature directly to mean translational kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Average Molecular Kinetic Energy
lessons.description: Link kelvin temperature to mean translational kinetic energy, compare gases and calculate rms speeds through worked microsteps.
learning_objectives: Obtain the mean translational kinetic-energy relation by comparing gas equations.
Use mean energy = three-halves kT in A2 calculations.
Compare energy and rms speed for different temperatures and particle masses.
Distinguish translational energy from complete internal energy.

slides.title: Link the two descriptions of pressure
slides.content:
The particle gas equation pV = NkT and the kinetic-theory equation pV = one-third Nm⟨c²⟩ describe the same ideal gas. Equate their right-hand sides. This lets us connect a macroscopic temperature measurement to the mean translational kinetic energy of one particle.

NkT = 13Nm⟨c²⟩

Divide by N, which is nonzero for a gas sample. Then multiply both sides by three-halves so that the right side becomes the kinetic-energy expression one-half m⟨c²⟩.

kT = 13m⟨c²⟩   ⇒   12m⟨c²⟩ = 32kT

Therefore the mean translational kinetic energy per particle, ⟨Ek,trans⟩, equals three-halves kT. Use T in K. In this lesson take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and, for Celsius inputs, T = θ + 273.

“Mean” matters: individual energies fluctuate across a distribution. “Translational” matters too: a molecule may also have rotational or vibrational energy. This equation does not assert that the total internal energy of every gas is three-halves NkT.

Tutor check-in

The formula three-halves kT gives:

slides.title: Worked example: a microscopic energy scale
slides.content:
Worked example 1: calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of a gas particle at 27 °C.

Step 1: Convert T = 27 + 273 = 300 K.

Step 2: Choose ⟨Ek,trans⟩ = 32kT.

Step 3: Substitute ⟨Ek,trans⟩ = 1.5 × (1.38 × 10⁻²³) × 300 = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Step 4: State this as a mean energy per particle, not a sample total.

Check: The unit is J because k has unit J K⁻¹. A very small energy per particle can still give a significant sample energy when multiplied by a very large particle count.

Heating from 300 K to 600 K doubles this mean energy. Heating from 20 °C to 40 °C does not: using the stated conversion, the ratio is 313 divided by 293, about 1.068. A temperature interval can be measured in °C, but a proportional-temperature law needs kelvin.

Tutor check-in

A gas warms from 300 K to 450 K. Its mean translational kinetic energy changes by a factor of:

slides.title: Worked example: infer temperature from energy
slides.content:
Worked example 2: an ideal-gas particle has mean translational kinetic energy 9.00 × 10⁻²¹ J. Find the gas temperature.

Step 1: Start with ⟨Ek,trans⟩ = three-halves kT.

Step 2: Multiply by two and divide by 3k: T = 2⟨Ek,trans⟩3k.

Step 3: Substitute T = 2 × 9.00 × 10⁻²¹3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ = 434.782… K.

Step 4: State T = 435 K to three significant figures.

Check: The numerator and denominator have units J and J K⁻¹, leaving K. Omitting the factor three-halves would overestimate T.

Particle mass is absent from this energy–temperature relation. At a common temperature, different species have the same mean translational energy even though their speeds differ. A heavier particle requires a smaller squared speed to have the same one-half mc² energy.

Tutor check-in

Helium and nitrogen are at the same temperature. Which mean quantity is equal?

slides.title: Equal temperature does not mean equal speed
slides.content:
Insert ⟨c²⟩ = crms² into the energy equation and rearrange. At fixed particle mass, rms speed is proportional to the square root of kelvin temperature. At fixed temperature, it is inversely proportional to the square root of particle mass.

crms = √(3kTm)

Worked example 3: calculate the rms speeds at 300 K for nitrogen of particle mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and helium of particle mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

Step 1: For nitrogen, crms² = 3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 3004.65 × 10⁻²⁶ = 2.67097… × 10⁵ m² s⁻².

Step 2: Taking the square root gives crms,N₂ = 516.8… ≈ 517 m s⁻¹.

Step 3: For helium, crms² = 3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 3006.64 × 10⁻²⁷ = 1.87048… × 10⁶ m² s⁻².

Step 4: Taking the square root gives crms,He ≈ 1370 m s⁻¹ to three significant figures.

Step 5: Both species still have ⟨Ek,trans⟩ = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J at 300 K.

Check: The lighter helium atom moves faster on average. Use the mass of one molecule or atom in kg, not its numerical molar mass.

slides.title: From a mean to a sample total: the stated model matters
slides.content:
For N particles, total translational kinetic energy is N times the mean: Etrans,total = three-halves NkT. For a monatomic ideal gas in this model, this is also its internal energy because the atoms have no molecular rotational or vibrational modes and intermolecular interaction energy is neglected.

Umonatomic ideal gas = 32NkT = 32nRT

For a diatomic gas such as nitrogen, translational energy is still three-halves NkT, but rotational and possibly vibrational contributions can make total U larger. Do not apply the monatomic internal-energy formula to every gas. The required molecular relationship here remains the translational one.

Worked example 4: 0.100 mol of a monatomic ideal gas is at 300 K. Find its internal energy using R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 1: The stated monatomic ideal model permits U = three-halves nRT.

Step 2: Substitute U = 1.5 × 0.100 × 8.31 × 300 = 373.95 J.

Step 3: Round U = 374 J.

Check: The result is a sample total, not an energy per atom. Doubling the amount at the same temperature would double U.

Tutor check-in

May three-halves NkT be used as the total internal energy of nitrogen without further assumptions?

slides.title: A2 practice: energy and temperature
slides.content:
These original A2-style questions use suggested teaching marks. Use k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Question 1: Mean energy [3 marks]

Find the mean translational kinetic energy at 400 K.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: ⟨Ek,trans⟩ = 1.5kT.

Step 2: ⟨Ek,trans⟩ = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 400 = 8.28 × 10⁻²¹ J per particle.

Question 2: Temperature from energy [4 marks]

The mean translational kinetic energy is 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J. Find T.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: T = 2⟨Ek,trans⟩3k.

Step 2: T = 2 × 4.14 × 10⁻²¹3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ = 200 K.

Question 3: Energy and speed ratios [4 marks]

An ideal gas warms from 300 K to 600 K at fixed particle mass. Compare its final mean translational energy and rms speed with the initial values.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Mean translational energy is proportional to T, so its final value is twice the initial value.

Step 2: Rms speed is proportional to √T at fixed mass, so its final value is √2 ≈ 1.41 times the initial value.

Step 3: Doubling energy does not double speed because kinetic energy depends on speed squared.

slides.title: A2 practice: compare particle masses
slides.content:
Question 4: Two species at equal temperature [4 marks]

At a common temperature, particle A has four times the mass of particle B. Find cᵣₘₛ,A divided by cᵣₘₛ,B and compare their mean translational energies.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: From crms = √(3kT divided by m), the speed ratio is √(mBmA).

Step 2: With mA = 4mB, the ratio is √(14) = 12.

Step 3: The heavier particle has half the rms speed, but both species have the same mean translational energy because their T values match.

Question 5: Total translational energy [4 marks]

A gas contains 2.00 × 10²² molecules at 300 K. Find its total translational kinetic energy. Explain why this need not be its complete internal energy.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Mean translational energy = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 = 6.21 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Step 2: Multiply by N: Etrans,total = (2.00 × 10²²)(6.21 × 10⁻²¹) = 124.2 J ≈ 124 J.

Step 3: Molecules may also have rotational and vibrational energy. The translational total alone need not equal their total internal energy.

Before moving on: identify whether an answer is per particle or for a sample, use kelvin, and distinguish energy ratios from speed ratios. Next, the limiting temperature 0 K gives the meaning of absolute zero.

lessons.title: Absolute Zero
lessons.description: Explain absolute zero, Celsius–kelvin conversion and gas-law extrapolation, including the limits of the classical model.
learning_objectives: State absolute zero as 0 K or −273.15 °C.
Convert individual temperatures and distinguish them from intervals.
Estimate an intercept from gas-law data and evaluate extrapolation.
Explain the classical thermal-energy interpretation without treating total internal energy as zero.

slides.title: The zero of the kelvin scale
slides.content:
Absolute zero is 0 K, equivalent to −273.15 °C. It is the lower limit of thermodynamic temperature for the ordinary equilibrium systems considered in this course. Kelvin is written K, with no degree symbol. A kelvin interval has the same size as a Celsius-degree interval, but the scales have different zero points.

T in K = θ in °C + 273.15

Use the exact offset 273.15 in this lesson. A question may permit 273 as a school approximation; follow its stated precision. Absolute-zero conversion is −273.15 °C, even when rounded gas-law arithmetic elsewhere uses 273.

Tutor check-in

Which notation is correct for absolute zero?

slides.title: Worked conversions and temperature intervals
slides.content:
Worked example 1: convert −40.00 °C into kelvin, and 250.00 K into degrees Celsius.

Step 1: For Celsius to kelvin, add 273.15: T = −40.00 + 273.15 = 233.15 K.

Step 2: For kelvin to Celsius, subtract 273.15: θ = 250.00 − 273.15 = −23.15 °C.

Step 3: Keep the signs explicit. A negative Celsius reading can still represent a positive kelvin temperature.

Check: Both temperatures are above absolute zero. A negative Celsius value does not mean negative thermodynamic temperature in this setting.

Worked example 2: a block warms from 18.0 °C to 53.0 °C. Find its rise in both temperature units.

Step 1: In Celsius, Δθ = 53.0 − 18.0 = 35.0 °C.

Step 2: The endpoints in kelvin are 291.15 K and 326.15 K.

Step 3: Subtract: ΔT = 326.15 − 291.15 = 35.0 K. The two offsets cancel.

Check: Convert individual temperatures for gas-law ratios. A temperature difference already has the same numerical value in °C and K.

Tutor check-in

A temperature rises by 12 °C. Its rise in kelvin is:

slides.title: How a gas experiment suggests the limiting zero
slides.content:
For a fixed mass of approximately ideal gas at constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature. If we plot pressure against Celsius temperature instead, the straight line can be extrapolated backwards until pressure would be zero. The intercept is near −273 °C. Constant-pressure volume data can be extrapolated in an analogous way.

This is an extrapolation of a model from accessible measurements. It is not a claim that the experiment reaches 0 K or that a real gas remains gaseous until its volume vanishes. Real gases condense as they cool, and their interactions become important. The simple ideal-gas line ceases to describe them accurately before the limiting intercept is reached.

Worked example 3: at fixed volume a gas has absolute pressure 100 kPa at 20 °C and 120 kPa at 80 °C. Use a straight-line approximation to estimate the Celsius temperature at zero pressure.

Step 1: The gradient is 120 − 10080 − 20 = 2060 = 0.3333… kPa per °C.

Step 2: To reduce pressure from 100 kPa to zero requires a temperature reduction of 1000.3333… = 300 °C.

Step 3: The intercept estimate is θ₀ = 20 − 300 = −280 °C.

Step 4: Compare with −273.15 °C: these rounded illustrative data give an approximate estimate, differing by 6.85 °C.

Check: Use the unrounded gradient. A small slope error can shift a long extrapolation substantially; this estimate does not redefine absolute zero.

In practice use many data points, a best-fit line and an uncertainty assessment. A pressure offset, gas outside the bath or a narrow temperature range can bias an intercept estimate.

Tutor check-in

Why can we not simply cool a real gas until its ideal extrapolated volume is zero?

slides.title: What “minimum motion” means in this course
slides.content:
The classical ideal-gas formula for mean translational kinetic energy, three-halves kT, tends to zero as T tends to 0 K. This gives the A2 thermal interpretation of absolute zero: the minimum limit of temperature-related random translational energy in that classical model.

Avoid claiming that all microscopic motion or all internal energy is literally zero. Interaction potential energy does not generally vanish at 0 K, and quantum systems can retain zero-point motion. This caveat matters when moving from the classical gas picture to real materials. NIST discusses the distinction between thermal motion and zero-point motion in its explanation of the kelvin.

NIST: the kelvin and absolute-zero interpretation

Worked example 4: an ideal gas warms from 0.00 °C to 100.00 °C. By what factor does its mean translational kinetic energy increase?

Step 1: Convert the endpoints: T₁ = 273.15 K and T₂ = 373.15 K.

Step 2: Mean translational kinetic energy is proportional to T, so the factor is 373.15273.15 = 1.3661… .

Step 3: The energy becomes about 1.37 times as large, an increase of about 36.6%.

Check: The initial energy is not zero at 0 °C. Taking a Celsius ratio would require division by zero and would be physically inappropriate.

Tutor check-in

Which statement about 0 K is most accurate?

slides.title: A2 practice: conversions and ratios
slides.content:
These original A2-style questions use suggested teaching marks. Use the exact 273.15 offset for this lesson.

Question 1: Two scale conversions [3 marks]

Convert −10.00 °C to kelvin and 200.00 K to degrees Celsius.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: T = −10.00 + 273.15 = 263.15 K.

Step 2: θ = 200.00 − 273.15 = −73.15 °C.

Question 2: A temperature interval [3 marks]

A sample cools from 40.0 °C to 15.0 °C. Give the temperature change and the magnitude of the fall in kelvin.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Change = final minus initial = 15.0 − 40.0 = −25.0 °C.

Step 2: The same signed change is −25.0 K. The magnitude of the fall is 25.0 K.

Question 3: Doubling absolute temperature [4 marks]

A gas is initially at 20.00 °C. Find the Celsius temperature at which its mean translational kinetic energy would double.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: T₁ = 293.15 K.

Step 2: Doubling the mean energy doubles kelvin temperature: T₂ = 586.30 K.

Step 3: θ₂ = 586.30 − 273.15 = 313.15 °C. Doubling the Celsius value would not meet the condition.

slides.title: A2 practice: extrapolation and explanation
slides.content:
Question 4: Find an intercept [5 marks]

A straight-line pressure–Celsius-temperature graph has equation p = 0.350θ + 95.6, where p is in kPa and θ is in °C. Estimate the zero-pressure temperature and give one reason it may differ from −273.15 °C.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Set p = 0: 0.350θ + 95.6 = 0.

Step 2: θ = −95.60.350 = −273.142… °C, approximately −273.1 °C.

Step 3: A pressure offset, gradient uncertainty or imperfect thermal equilibrium can shift the fitted intercept. These are possible experimental limitations; the intercept does not alter the definition of 0 K.

Question 5: Explain the limit [4 marks]

Explain how gas-law graphs suggest absolute zero and why this does not establish that every real particle becomes completely stationary there.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: At fixed volume, ideal-gas absolute pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature. Extrapolating pressure against Celsius temperature gives a zero-pressure intercept near −273.15 °C.

Step 2: Real gases condense and leave the ideal regime before that extrapolated point.

Step 3: The classical thermal translational-energy relation tends to zero at 0 K, but real quantum systems can have zero-point motion and nonzero interaction energy.

Before continuing: distinguish an individual temperature from an interval, explain why ratios use K, and interpret a gas-law intercept as an extrapolation. The final lesson uses temperature changes to measure specific heat capacity.
