lessons.title: Specific Heat Capacity
lessons.description: Measure specific heat capacity electrically, use Q = mcΔθ, and evaluate heat losses, heating graphs and uncertainty.
learning_objectives: Define specific heat capacity and distinguish it from sample heat capacity.
Use Q = mcΔθ and electrical input energy in A2 calculations.
Describe an electrical measurement method with meaningful controls.
Analyse heating gradients, heat-loss bias and maximum propagated uncertainty.

slides.title: Why equal energy inputs give different temperature rises
slides.content:
A kettle and a small metal spoon do not warm by the same amount when given equal energy. The rise depends on the material and on how much of it is present. Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed per unit mass for a unit temperature rise, without a change of state.

Q = mcΔθ    and    c = QmΔθ

Here Q is energy gained by the material in J, m is mass in kg and Δθ is its temperature rise. The SI unit of c is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A temperature change has the same numerical value in K and °C, so a measured rise of 10 °C is 10 K. Do not add 273 to a rise.

The equation assumes that the material remains in one state and that c is approximately constant over the chosen interval. Energy supplied during melting or boiling cannot be calculated from a zero temperature rise using this equation. Q means energy actually gained by the material; an electrical heater’s input may be larger because of losses.

Tutor check-in

A block warms from 20 °C to 45 °C. Which Δθ belongs in Q = mcΔθ?

slides.title: Specific heat capacity versus heat capacity
slides.content:
Specific heat capacity is a property per kilogram. Heat capacity C belongs to a particular object or sample: it is the energy needed to raise that whole sample by 1 K. The connection is C = mc, with C in J K⁻¹. Doubling the mass doubles C, while c is unchanged for the same material under the same conditions.

Worked example 1: a 0.500 kg block has c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the energy needed for a rise from 18.0 °C to 58.0 °C and its heat capacity.

Step 1: Find Δθ = 58.0 − 18.0 = 40.0 K.

Step 2: Use Q = mcΔθ = 0.500 × 900 × 40.0 = 18000 J = 18.0 kJ.

Step 3: Calculate heat capacity C = mc = 0.500 × 900 = 450 J K⁻¹.

Step 4: Interpret C: this block needs approximately 450 J per kelvin rise if losses are negligible.

Check: The unit kg cancels the per-kilogram factor in c. A larger block of the same material needs proportionally more energy.

Worked example 2: 0.200 kg of a material of c = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ receives 3600 J with negligible losses. Find its temperature rise.

Step 1: Divide Q = mcΔθ by mc: Δθ = Qmc.

Step 2: Substitute Δθ = 36000.200 × 450 = 360090.0 = 40.0 K.

Step 3: This is also a rise of 40.0 °C. To find a final temperature, add the rise to a separately given initial temperature.

Check: A rise is not an absolute temperature. Without the initial reading, the final temperature cannot be found.

Tutor check-in

Two blocks of the same material have masses m and 2m. If given equal retained energy, the heavier block has:

slides.title: The electrical method: apparatus and measured quantities
slides.content:
Use a metal block of known material with separate bores for an electrical heater and a temperature probe. Measure the block’s mass on a balance before adding insulation. Fit the heater fully into its bore and the probe securely into the other bore. A small approved amount of thermal-contact medium, following the apparatus instructions, improves contact and reduces temperature lag.

Wrap the block in suitable insulation, leaving connections accessible. Connect the heater to a low-voltage supply through a joulemeter. The joulemeter measures the total electrical energy delivered to the heater. Alternatively measure potential difference across the heater, current through it and heating time; then Ein = VIt for steady values. In this practical V denotes electrical potential difference, rather than gas volume.

The recorded quantities are mass m, initial and final temperatures, and electrical input Ein. The estimated c is Ein divided by mΔθ when losses and energy stored in the heater or probe are small. Those assumptions must be checked and discussed, rather than hidden by the calculation.

Use the low-voltage apparatus within its rating, keep leads secure, switch off before moving the heater, and avoid touching the hot block. Keep electrical connections dry if using a liquid sample. These precautions follow directly from the equipment and heating involved.

slides.title: A method you can describe and evaluate
slides.content:
Record the mass with its instrument resolution. With the supply off, allow the block and probe to settle near a uniform initial temperature; record θ₁. Zero the joulemeter. Switch on the heater, maintain a steady input and record temperature and accumulated energy at regular intervals. Keep the heater and probe positions and insulation unchanged.

Continue until a measurable temperature rise has been obtained without overheating or changing state. Switch off and record the final energy. Account for probe response and thermal equilibration consistently: a delayed temperature rise can reflect energy moving from the heater into the block, while a long wait also permits extra losses. A temperature–time record helps identify this lag rather than choosing an arbitrary final reading.

Calculate Δθ = θ₂ − θ₁ and cestimate = Ein divided by mΔθ. Repeat after returning to comparable initial conditions. Repeats show variability; changing the insulation or using a more appropriate temperature interval can investigate a systematic heat-loss effect.

State the key controls: same block mass and material, consistent heater/probe contact, steady power where VIt is used, comparable initial conditions and insulation. A thermometer measures its own sensor temperature, so good thermal contact and sufficient equilibration are essential.

Tutor check-in

Which measurement is essential even when a joulemeter gives the energy directly?

slides.title: Worked example: find c from an electrical input
slides.content:
Worked example 3: a 0.500 kg block is heated at 12.0 V with a steady current of 2.00 A for 120 s. Its temperature rises by 6.00 K. Estimate c, initially assuming all electrical input warms the block.

Step 1: Calculate power P = VI = 12.0 × 2.00 = 24.0 W.

Step 2: Calculate input energy Ein = Pt = 24.0 × 120 = 2880 J.

Step 3: Assume Q ≈ Ein and rearrange c = QmΔθ.

Step 4: Substitute c = 28800.500 × 6.00 = 960 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 5: Label the answer as an estimate based on negligible losses and negligible heater/probe heat capacity.

Check: The denominator is 3.00 kg K. Its units leave J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, not J K⁻¹.

If voltage or current varies, a single VIt product may misrepresent the input. Record their changes or use an appropriate joulemeter that accumulates energy. A larger electrical input is not proof that the block retained all of it.

Tutor check-in

A student reports 960 J K⁻¹ as the specific heat capacity in this example. What is missing?

slides.title: Heat losses: predict the direction of the error
slides.content:
Some input energy can warm the heater, probe or insulation, or leave by conduction, convection and radiation. If you put the full electrical input into Q = mcΔθ while only part warmed the block, the numerator is too large for the measured rise. The estimated c is therefore usually too high for the block alone.

Better insulation reduces loss, but does not establish zero loss. Keeping the block closer to room temperature reduces the temperature difference driving outward transfer. A longer heating run gives a larger measurable rise but may increase total heat loss. Choose a useful interval that balances relative reading uncertainty, response lag and loss, rather than claiming “heat for as long as possible”.

Worked example 4: a 0.500 kg block receives 18000 J of electrical input and rises by 40.0 K. A separate estimate shows 2000 J went elsewhere. Find the corrected c and compare it with the uncorrected value.

Step 1: Energy gained by the block is Q = 18000 − 2000 = 16000 J.

Step 2: Corrected c = 160000.500 × 40.0 = 800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 3: Using all input would give cuncorrected = 180000.500 × 40.0 = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 4: The uncorrected value is 100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ too high, or 12.5% above the corrected value.

Check: Subtract the lost or otherwise stored energy before calculating the block’s c. Heat loss makes the measured rise smaller for a given input.

Tutor check-in

If outward losses are ignored, the estimated c for the block is usually:

slides.title: Use a temperature–time graph
slides.content:
At steady power P, energy delivered over an interval Δt is PΔt. If this energy warms the block, PΔt = mcΔθ. Dividing by Δt gives P = mc × gradient, where the gradient is Δθ divided by Δt. The unit is K s⁻¹, numerically the same as °C s⁻¹.

gradient = ΔθΔt = Pmc   ⇒   c = Pm × gradient

Worked example 5: a 0.500 kg block is heated at 24.0 W. A best-fit straight section rises by 4.80 K over 90.0 s. Find c, assuming negligible losses in that section.

Step 1: Find gradient = 4.8090.0 = 0.053333… K s⁻¹.

Step 2: Use c = P divided by the product of mass and gradient.

Step 3: Substitute c = 24.00.500 × 0.053333… = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Check: Use a large triangle on the best-fit line and retain extra digits. The graph method and energy method follow the same equation.

An early lag can come from imperfect contact and heater/probe response. Later flattening can result from increasing loss as the block gets hotter. Use a justified region after the initial response; do not assume every point belongs to a loss-free straight line. A later shallow gradient, used with full input power, tends to overestimate c.

Tutor check-in

At the same mass and power, a material has twice c. Its ideal heating gradient is:

slides.title: Estimate uncertainty and improve the measurement
slides.content:
A temperature rise uses two readings. For a maximum uncertainty estimate, add their absolute reading uncertainties before finding the percentage uncertainty in the difference. A small rise can therefore have a large relative uncertainty even if the thermometer resolution seems fine.

δ(Δθ) = δθ₁ + δθ₂

For c = Q divided by mΔθ, add the percentage uncertainties in Q, m and Δθ as a maximum propagated estimate. This differs from a statistical combination of independent standard uncertainties. State the method being used; it does not automatically include heat-loss bias or calibration errors.

δcc ≈ δQQ + δmm + δ(Δθ)Δθ

Worked example 6: Q = 9000 ± 180 J, m = 0.500 ± 0.005 kg and Δθ = 20.0 K. Each of the two temperature readings has uncertainty ±0.1 K. Estimate the maximum uncertainty in c.

Step 1: Calculate c = 90000.500 × 20.0 = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 2: The rise uncertainty is ±(0.1 + 0.1) = ±0.2 K, giving 0.220.0 × 100% = 1.0%.

Step 3: Energy uncertainty is 2.0% and mass uncertainty is 1.0%. Add them with the rise uncertainty: 4.0%.

Step 4: Absolute uncertainty in c is 0.040 × 900 = 36 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Report approximately 900 ± 40 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ after sensible uncertainty rounding.

Check: Repeats do not remove systematic heat loss. The propagated estimate applies to the stated reading uncertainties.

A fixed thermometer zero offset cancels when the same instrument is used for both readings, but a scale-factor error or changing drift may remain. Better resolution helps a small rise; better contact and insulation address different problems. Explain each improvement by connecting it to its error source.

slides.title: A2 practice: energy, c and heat losses
slides.content:
These are original A2-style questions with suggested teaching marks. Assume one phase and approximately constant c unless stated otherwise.

Question 1: Energy for heating [4 marks]

Find the energy needed to warm 0.750 kg of water by 12.0 K. Take c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and negligible losses.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Q = mcΔθ = 0.750 × 4200 × 12.0.

Step 2: Q = 37800 J = 37.8 kJ. The rise is already a temperature interval and needs no offset.

Question 2: Electrical estimate [5 marks]

A 0.400 kg block is heated at 10.0 V and 1.80 A for 100 s. Its temperature rises by 10.0 K. Estimate c with negligible losses.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Power = VI = 18.0 W; input energy = VIt = 1800 J.

Step 2: c = 18000.400 × 10.0 = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 3: This assumes the input energy warms the block, with negligible losses and negligible extra heat capacity.

Question 3: Correct for a loss [5 marks]

In Question 2, suppose 180 J of the input went elsewhere. Find the corrected c and explain the direction of the original error.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Block energy Q = 1800 − 180 = 1620 J.

Step 2: c = 16200.400 × 10.0 = 405 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 3: The original 450 value is too high because it assigns energy that did not warm the block to the block’s temperature rise.

slides.title: A2 practice: graphs, uncertainty and method
slides.content:
Question 4: Heating gradient [5 marks]

A 0.600 kg block is heated at 15.0 W. Its steady straight-line temperature rise is 3.00 K in 120 s. Find c and explain how increasing heat loss would affect the estimate.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Gradient = 3.00120 = 0.0250 K s⁻¹.

Step 2: c = 15.00.600 × 0.0250 = 1000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Step 3: Increasing loss reduces the rise rate for the same input power. Using that reduced gradient with the full power would overestimate c.

Question 5: Uncertainty in a small rise [4 marks]

Temperature readings have uncertainty ±0.2 K each and give a rise of 4.0 K. Find the maximum percentage uncertainty in the rise. Suggest an improvement and its tradeoff.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Rise uncertainty = ±0.4 K by adding the two absolute reading uncertainties.

Step 2: Percentage uncertainty = 0.44.0 × 100% = 10%.

Step 3: A greater rise reduces this relative reading uncertainty, but heating further can increase outward loss. A finer thermometer can reduce reading uncertainty without requiring such a large rise.

Question 6: Describe and evaluate the practical [6 marks]

Describe an electrical method to measure a metal’s specific heat capacity. Include the measurements, calculation and two improvements linked to limitations.

Reveal worked solution

Step 1: Measure the block mass. Insert a heater and probe with good thermal contact, insulate the block and record its initial temperature.

Step 2: Use a low-voltage supply and joulemeter, or steady V, I and timed heating. Record input energy and the temperature rise.

Step 3: Calculate c ≈ Ein divided by mΔθ, stating that losses and heater/probe heat capacity are assumed small.

Step 4: Improve insulation to reduce outward loss; improve contact and analyse a temperature–time record to reduce or recognise lag. Repeat from comparable starting conditions to assess variability.

Thermal Physics review: gas laws describe how p, V, T and amount are linked; kinetic theory explains pressure and temperature through microscopic motion; internal energy includes microscopic kinetic and potential contributions; specific heat capacity connects retained energy to a temperature change. Keep model assumptions, reference scales and units visible in your working.
